The Diskless-fingered odorous frog, Odorrana grahami, is a mid-sized ranid endemic to montane streams of southwestern China. Data from the closely related congener Odorrana swinhoana provide useful estimates for several life-history traits of this poorly known species. For instance, the incubation period for embryos, maintained at a constant temperature of 19 °C [T = 19 °C], is approximately 45 days [ab = approximately 45 days], a duration that aligns with the protracted development often observed in cold-adapted stream-breeding amphibians. Newly hatched larvae emerge at a remarkably small size, with a wet weight at birth of just 0.0141 grams [Wwb = 0.0141 grams], reflecting the tiny, yolk-rich eggs from which they originate. This initial mass is coupled with a snout-vent length at metamorphosis of 2.3 centimeters , a figure that marks the transition from the aquatic larval stage to the terrestrial juvenile phase. The larval period itself involves substantial growth and morphological transformation, including the development of hind limbs and the resorption of the tail, all of which are highly temperature-dependent.

Following metamorphosis, growing juveniles of Odorrana grahami experience a prolonged period of somatic development before reaching reproductive maturity. Field-based growth models, anchored by data from O. swinhoana, indicate that females attain sexual maturity at a snout-vent length of 6 centimeters [Lp = 6 centimeters], while males begin to mature at a slightly smaller size of 5 centimeters [Lp = 5 centimeters]. The time required to reach this pubertal stage from birth, when reared under the thermal regime of 19 °C [T = 19 °C], is approximately 365 days from birth [tp = approximately 365 days from birth]. This one-year interval to puberty is a relatively rapid pace for a ranid frog of this size, suggesting that the species may prioritize early maturation in its stable, cool-stream environment. The onset of gonadal activity marks a critical shift in physiological investment, as resources are increasingly directed toward gametogenesis and the development of secondary sexual characteristics rather than further linear growth.

The ultimate body size attained by adult Odorrana grahami is strongly dimorphic between the sexes, a common pattern among ranid frogs where females are the larger sex. Based on projections from the well-studied Odorrana swinhoana, the maximum snout-vent length for females is estimated at 11.3 centimeters [Li = 11.3 centimeters], whereas males reach a more modest ultimate length of 8.8 centimeters [Li = 8.8 centimeters]. This size disparity is reflected even more strikingly in body mass, as volumetric scaling dictates that the ultimate wet weight for females is approximately 132.6 grams [Wwi = approximately 132.6 grams], more than double the 62.6 grams [Wwi = 62.6 grams] predicted for mature males. Such a pronounced difference in adult body mass likely has significant implications for reproductive output, as larger females can accommodate a greater clutch volume and produce larger, more viable eggs. The selective pressures driving this dimorphism are probably linked to fecundity advantages for females and possibly male-male competition for breeding sites within the torrential stream habitat.

In Odorrana grahami, the gonadosomatic index (GSI) is estimated at approximately 15% [GSI = approximately 15%] at the species' typical active temperature of 19 °C [T = 19 °C]. This value indicates that the ovaries of a breeding female constitute about fifteen percent of her total body mass, a moderate level of reproductive allocation compared to other stream-breeding anurans. The timing of the first reproductive event is not yet precisely documented for this species, but it is thought to occur soon after the attainment of sexual maturity. The life-history strategy appears to favor iteroparity, with adults potentially breeding annually. The maximum lifespan recorded for individuals under these stable thermal conditions is approximately 5 years [am = approximately 5 years], although longevity in the wild may be constrained by predation and the energetic demands of surviving the dry season at a temperature of 19 °C [T = 19 °C].

Comparative analysis of the life-history traits of Odorrana grahami reveals a strategy that is intermediate between explosive breeders and prolonged breeders. The relatively short time to maturity from birth of one year (1 year from birth) [tp = 1 year from birth] suggests a reliance on stable recruitment rather than a single large reproductive pulse at a temperature of 19 °C [T = 19 °C]. The small size at metamorphosis of 2.3 centimeters  indicates that the aquatic larval phase is not unusually prolonged, which is somewhat surprising given the cool, well-oxygenated streams it inhabits. The adult body mass of 132.6 grams [Wwi = 132.6 grams] for females and 62.6 grams [Wwi = 62.6 grams] for males positions the species as a medium-sized ranid, with a body plan adapted for clinging to slippery rocks in fast-flowing water. The absence of digital discs, a defining feature of the genus Odorrana, is compensated by well-developed toe pads and friction ridges. The species’ reliance on cool, constant-temperature springs likely buffers it against extreme climatic variation, but also restricts its distribution. Further field studies are required to confirm the reproductive frequency and clutch parameters of this fascinating but understudied amphibian.
